div.note: Liebermann prints D (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 201, p. 101, after the Canons of Edgar, c. 1060) and H (Textus Roffensis f. 93, after VI As, same hand, c. 1120), with the Quadripartitus and the Instituta Cnuti III 60–63.1. K is H; D is also given here. H's heading is in red; D's is probably not original (perhaps referring to Norðleod and Mirce). Liebermann notes that Geþyncðo, Norðleod, Mirce, Að and Had stand only in MSS going back to one archetype before c. 1060, which held them in this order; they show traces of composition after 1027, perhaps by one hand, and Geþyncðo may be meant as an introduction to the next two pieces. He dates Geþyncðo c. 1029–c. 1060. The language is in places raised by rhythm and alliteration. Clause number standardised from ‘Geþyncðo Inscr.’.; AU: corrected against Rabin p. 10 / 11, October 2026 (was “Be leode geþincðum and lage”, now “Be leode geþincðum and lage (expanded letters in italics: Be leode geþincðum and lage)”); AA: corrected against Rabin p. 10 / 11, October 2026 (was “On the Ranks of People and Law”, now “On the Ranks of People and Law (expanded letters in italics: On the Ranks of People and Law)”); AY: corrected against Rabin p. 10 / 11, October 2026 (was “∅; Be . . . lage: Be wergildum and be geðinðum D”, now “Be . . . lage: Be wergildum and be geðinðum D; ∅”); AT: added from Whitelock p. 476, October 2026 (Whitelock’s footnotes); F: corrected against Liebermann, Gesetze I (date in the running heads), October 2026 (was “1002–23 (Whitelock); 1006–8 (Rabin)”, now “c.1029–c.1060 (Liebermann); 1002–23 (Whitelock); 1006–8 (Rabin)”); F: corrected against Liebermann, Gesetze I (date at the head of the text); Wormald, Making of English Law I; Whitelock, English Historical Documents I, October 2026 (was “c.1029–c.1060 (Liebermann); 1002–23 (Whitelock); 1006–8 (Rabin)”, now “c.1029–c.1060 (Liebermann, I p. 456); 1002–23 (Whitelock, EHD p. 475); 1006–8 (Rabin)”); BQ: page of each of Liebermann’s texts and of his German, checked against Liebermann, Gesetze I (our double-read transcription), October 2026 (e.g. was “(empty)”, now “D 456; H 456; Q 457; German 457”; 9 rows of Geþyncðo)

The text here is based on that in Textus Roffensis, though Wulfstan’s original order has been preserved. Significant variants from Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MSS 190 and 201 have been identified in the notes.

note.seg: Die fünf folgenden Stücke Geþyncðo, Norðleod, Mirce, Að, Had stehen nur in Hss., welche zurückgehen auf Einen Archetyp vor c. 1060, der sie so geordnet enthielt. Sie verrathen neben älteren Kernen Spuren von Abfassung nach 1027, vielleicht durch Eine Hand. Vielleicht will Geþyncþo als Einleitung dienen zu den folgenden zwei Stücken, die im Wesentlichen eine frühere Schrift copiren

The five following pieces Geþyncðo, Norðleod, Mirce, Að, Had occur only in MSS that go back to a single archetype before c. 1060, which contained them in this order. Alongside older cores they betray traces of composition after 1027, perhaps by a single hand. Perhaps Geþyncþo is meant to serve as an introduction to the following two pieces, which essentially copy an earlier text

note.seg: Die beiden Klassen der Hss. haben die Wörter Be geþyncðum gemeinsam. Diese, aus c. 1. entnommen, dürfen alse sicher für archetyp gelten. Vielleicht standen sie einst allein.—Was D davor setzt, bezieht sich nämlich auf die hinter dem ersten folgenden Stücke; möglich also, dass D's Rubrik deren ganze Sammlung umfassen wollte. Und was H hinzufügt, scheint nur aus c. 1 Z. 1 geschöpft. Vielleicht nur aus dem Lateinischen Quadripartitus-Text schöpft hier (wie sicher oft) die nur in letzter Rezension auftauchende Überschrift in Q; zwar könnte promotiones : geþyncðo übersetzen wollen; allein Q missverstand das Wort 1{b}.—Das Kompositum leodgeþincð ist nur Thorpes Erfindung

The two classes of MSS have the words Be geþyncðum in common. These, taken from c. 1., may be regarded as certainly belonging to the archetype. Perhaps they once stood alone.—For what D places before them refers to the pieces that follow after the first; it is possible, then, that D’s rubric was meant to cover their whole collection. And what H adds seems to be drawn only from c. 1 l. 1. The heading in Q, which appears only in the last recension, perhaps draws here (as it certainly often does) only on the Latin Quadripartitus text; promotiones might indeed be intended to translate geþyncðo; but Q misunderstood the word 1{b}.—The compound leodgeþincð is merely Thorpe’s invention

The texts I include under this heading are those called by Liebermann Geþyncðo, Norðleoda laga, Mircna laga. Að and Hadbot, and printed by him, I, 456–69. Thorpe has the three first, in a different order, I, 186–93. The five texts occur in C.C.C.C., MS. 201, a manuscript with connections with Archbishop Wulfstan, and D.Bethurum has produced good reasons for assigning the collection to this prelate, who was deeply interested in this matter. The last three are also in C.C.C.C.. MS. 190, another manuscript connected with Wulfstan. All five, but not as a group or in order, are in the Textus Roffensis, and the authors of Quadripartitus and the Instituta Cnuti use them. Much of what is known of status in Anglo-Saxon times comes from these texts, which should not be regarded as official enactments but as a private compilation. [Her footnote 2: No. 52 in the 1955 edition] [Her footnote 3: Journ. Engl. and Germ. Phil., xlix, 449–63]
